product.name: Get Clarity Assessment
product.subtitle: by Clarity Engine
product.tagline: See what's working. Find what's holding you back. Know what to do next.

patterns.title: Foundational Offer Clarity
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: sales/offer acceptance; Supporting: qualified lead rate; Diagnostic: objection frequency
patterns.workSession: What have people repeatedly paid for? What problem are they hiring you to solve? Which offer would you keep if only one survived?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Synthesize services, testimonials, and sales language into 3–5 possible offer formulations.

patterns.title: Market Validation Warning
patterns.triggerDescription: O5 D/E regardless of average Offer score
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: sales/offer acceptance; Supporting: qualified interest; Diagnostic: objections/rejection themes
patterns.workSession: What direct evidence proves demand? What behavior supports assumptions? What are prospects actually rejecting?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Analyze interview transcripts for repeated motivations, objections, unmet needs, and language.

patterns.title: Audience Definition Constraint
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: qualified customer/lead rate; Supporting: conversion by segment; Diagnostic: fit patterns
patterns.workSession: Who gets the most value? What changes right before they seek help? Who should not be targeted?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Cluster CRM or transcript data into meaningful customer groups and buying triggers.

patterns.title: Lead Quality Problem
patterns.triggerDescription: A3 D/E while traffic/lead volume is not clearly deficient
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: qualified lead rate; Supporting: close rate; Diagnostic: CPL by source/segment
patterns.workSession: What separates strong from weak leads? Which sources create customers rather than forms?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Categorize recent leads into quality tiers and identify common traits/source patterns.

patterns.title: Strong Offer, Weak Message
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: conversion rate; Supporting: CTA click rate; Diagnostic: CTR/engagement
patterns.workSession: What does the customer actually want? What phrases do they use? What would a stranger understand in five seconds?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Use current hero, offer, testimonials, and customer language to generate distinct messaging territories and hero options.

patterns.title: Differentiation / Positioning Gap
patterns.triggerDescription: M4 D/E while Offer/Audience are reasonably strong
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: sales conversion; Supporting: CTA rate; Diagnostic: objection themes
patterns.workSession: Why choose you? What do customers get here they cannot easily get elsewhere? What alternative are they really comparing you to?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Compare company messaging with competitor pages and identify interchangeable claims and differentiation territories.

patterns.title: Trust / Credibility Constraint
patterns.triggerDescription: M6 and/or C5 D/E, especially with meaningful commitment/high-ticket offer
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: conversion rate; Supporting: CTA→conversion rate; Diagnostic: engagement around proof/decision areas
patterns.workSession: What claims need proof? What evidence already exists? Where does hesitation occur?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Turn reviews, testimonials, results, and project notes into concise proof modules or case-card drafts.

patterns.title: Conversion Experience Constraint
patterns.triggerDescription: Conversion <55 while upstream Offer/Message are reasonably functional
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: page/funnel conversion rate; Supporting: CTA click rate; Diagnostic: drop-off by step
patterns.caseFormat: Before → After; youth-sports/free-trial style where applicable
patterns.workSession: Map every click/page/field. What can be removed? Where does trust drop?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Audit a page section-by-section against one conversion goal and identify ambiguity, redundancy, and friction.

patterns.title: Commitment Mismatch
patterns.triggerDescription: C6 D/E plus contextual evidence that ask and journey are misaligned
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: completion/conversion rate; Supporting: CTA rate; Diagnostic: abandonment point
patterns.workSession: What are you asking the visitor to risk—time, money, data, commitment—and does the surrounding experience justify it?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Compare the size of the ask to the current process and generate simplification or trust-building options.

patterns.title: More-Traffic Trap
patterns.triggerDescription: Meaningful upstream weakness in Offer/Message/Conversion plus scale intent or O6 D/E
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: KPI associated with upstream constraint; Supporting: current CVR; Diagnostic: traffic quality
patterns.workSession: Why do you believe more traffic is the answer? What would happen if traffic doubled tomorrow?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Use AI to accelerate diagnosis/ideation of the upstream issue rather than create more campaign volume.
planPhases: Learn: validate and reassess scale readiness

patterns.title: True Traffic Constraint
patterns.triggerDescription: Offer ≥75, Audience ≥75, Message ≥70, Conversion ≥70, Traffic <60, Measurement sufficiently trustworthy
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: CAC/CPA/qualified customer volume; Supporting: conversion rate; Diagnostic: CTR/CPC/reach/impression share as relevant
patterns.workSession: Where does existing demand come from? Which channel gives the clearest next test? What can you afford to acquire?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Research and brainstorm channel hypotheses, messaging angles, and creative concepts before choosing the subset worth funding.

patterns.title: Channel-Role Mismatch
patterns.triggerDescription: T1 + T4 weak and multiple acquisition channels exist
deprioritizedActions: Declaring channels failures from last-click results
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: revenue/qualified acquisition; Supporting: assisted/return conversion behavior; Diagnostic: role-specific channel metrics
patterns.workSession: What job is each channel actually performing? Where is discovery occurring? Where is conversion occurring?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Summarize multi-touch journeys/reporting exports into role hypotheses and flag where attribution may be misleading.

patterns.title: Underpowered Testing
patterns.triggerDescription: T5 D/E and/or testing fragmentation plus limited budget/conversion volume
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: target outcome of the test; Supporting: conversion volume; Diagnostic: spend/data per variant
patterns.workSession: What single question is most valuable to answer? What baseline are you protecting? What evidence would cause you to keep/reject the change?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Generate many hypotheses cheaply, score them for expected impact/ease/evidence, then select the best 1–3 for real-world testing.

patterns.title: Attribution / Data Trust Constraint
patterns.triggerDescription: ML4 D/E and/or ML5 D/E with active acquisition
deprioritizedActions: Large budget shifts from platform-only attribution
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: authoritative business-source outcome; Supporting: qualified lead/purchase volume; Diagnostic: platform-vs-source discrepancies
patterns.caseFormat: Business Model → Constraint → Priority; travel attribution where applicable
patterns.workSession: Which numbers decide whether marketing is actually working? Where does each come from? Where does visibility disappear?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Reconcile exports from ad platforms, CRM, ecommerce, or sales systems and identify mismatches/gaps.

patterns.title: Follow-Up Leakage
patterns.triggerDescription: Traffic exists, consideration is non-trivial, follow-up/nurture is missing or weak based on context and responses
patterns.kpiGuidance: Primary: lead/visitor-to-sale rate over time; Supporting: return/nurture conversion; Diagnostic: email/retargeting engagement
patterns.workSession: What happens to the people who do not convert immediately? What useful next touchpoint should they receive?
patterns.aiAccelerator: Turn offer/customer context into nurture sequences, retargeting angles, and segmented follow-up ideas.

recommendations.title: Write your primary offer in one sentence.
recommendations.whatToDo: Explain who it is for, what they get, and what changes for them.
recommendations.whyCritical: If a potential customer cannot quickly understand what you sell, every ad, landing page, sales conversation, and referral has to work harder just to establish basic clarity.

recommendations.title: Identify the single most important customer outcome.
recommendations.whatToDo: Decide what one result the customer should remember above everything else.
recommendations.whyCritical: Without a clear outcome, buyers are more likely to evaluate your features, deliverables, or price instead of understanding the larger value they are buying.

recommendations.title: Simplify competing offers.
recommendations.whatToDo: Choose one primary offer and make secondary offers clearly secondary.
recommendations.whyCritical: When several offers compete for attention, customers have to decide what matters before they can decide whether to buy. One clear primary offer reduces that decision burden.

recommendations.title: Review the last 10 sales conversations.
recommendations.whatToDo: Identify why people bought, hesitated, said no, and what they expected to receive.

recommendations.title: Interview five recent customers.
recommendations.whatToDo: Ask what problem they were trying to solve, what triggered action, and why they chose you.

recommendations.title: Validate demand before scaling.
recommendations.whatToDo: Put the offer in front of real prospects before investing heavily in traffic.

recommendations.title: Strengthen the reason to act now.
recommendations.whatToDo: Clarify why the problem, opportunity, or timing deserves attention without fake scarcity.

recommendations.title: Review pricing against perceived value.
recommendations.whatToDo: Assess price relative to outcome, alternatives, proof, and commitment.

recommendations.title: Categorize your last 20–50 leads.
recommendations.whatToDo: Group them by fit, quality, revenue potential, source, and outcome.

recommendations.title: Identify your highest-value customer segment.
recommendations.whatToDo: Determine which group combines the strongest revenue, retention, margin, referrals, or ease of sale.

recommendations.title: Document top purchase triggers.
recommendations.whatToDo: Identify what tends to happen immediately before someone looks for what you sell.

recommendations.title: Map audience → problem → trigger → channel.
recommendations.whatToDo: For each meaningful segment, document who they are, what they feel, what makes them act, and where to reach them.

recommendations.title: Interview three ideal customers.
recommendations.whatToDo: Focus on language, frustrations, alternatives considered, and what made the decision worthwhile.

recommendations.title: Separate poor-fit leads from poor marketing.
recommendations.whatToDo: If inquiries are bad fits, refine targeting or qualification before increasing volume.

recommendations.title: Identify who is not a fit.
recommendations.whatToDo: Define exclusion criteria as clearly as inclusion criteria.

recommendations.title: Match customer segment to message.
recommendations.whatToDo: If groups buy for different reasons, stop showing every audience the same message.

recommendations.title: Rewrite the hero section around the customer outcome.
recommendations.whatToDo: Rewrite the hero section of your homepage or primary landing page(s) so it is centered around the customer’s primary outcome, not just your company, service, or process.

recommendations.title: Replace feature language with benefit language.
recommendations.whatToDo: For every major feature, state what it allows the customer to do, avoid, gain, or feel.

recommendations.title: Extract customer language from real conversations.
recommendations.whatToDo: Review sales calls, testimonials, reviews, emails, and support questions for repeated language.

recommendations.title: Clarify why someone should choose you.
recommendations.whatToDo: Identify 2–3 meaningful differentiators that matter to the customer.

recommendations.title: Add proof immediately after major claims.
recommendations.whatToDo: Support claims with results, reviews, testimonials, examples, credentials, or demonstrations.

recommendations.title: Create one emotional hook and one rational hook.
recommendations.whatToDo: Develop both an emotional reason to care and a rational reason to believe.

recommendations.title: Audit message consistency across the journey.
recommendations.whatToDo: Compare ad → landing page → form → sales call → checkout for continuity.

recommendations.title: Remove internal jargon.
recommendations.whatToDo: Rewrite language that makes sense internally but forces a new customer to translate it.

recommendations.title: Choose one primary conversion action.
recommendations.whatToDo: Make one next step visually and conceptually dominant.

recommendations.title: Put the value proposition and CTA earlier.
recommendations.whatToDo: Do not make visitors search for what they get or what to do next.

recommendations.title: Reduce unnecessary conversion steps.
recommendations.whatToDo: Map every click, page, field, form, and confirmation; remove what does not materially help.

recommendations.title: Match the experience to the size of the ask.
recommendations.whatToDo: Low-risk actions should feel easy; high-commitment actions need more trust and context.

recommendations.title: Move proof closer to the decision point.
recommendations.whatToDo: Place the strongest reassurance near high-friction actions.

recommendations.title: Establish your baseline conversion rate.
recommendations.whatToDo: Know the current conversion rate before redesigning everything.

recommendations.title: Test the first screen before redesigning the whole page.
recommendations.whatToDo: Start with headline, subheadline, CTA, proof, and offer clarity.

recommendations.title: Review the experience on mobile.
recommendations.whatToDo: Confirm CTA visibility, form usability, readability, load time, and low distraction.

recommendations.title: Map each channel to its role in the funnel.
recommendations.whatToDo: Define whether each channel contributes to discovery, intent capture, retargeting, nurture, conversion, or reactivation.

recommendations.title: Separate traffic volume from traffic quality.
recommendations.whatToDo: Measure which sources create qualified business outcomes, not just clicks or forms.

recommendations.title: Build a prospecting + retargeting structure.
recommendations.whatToDo: Where appropriate, separate new audience acquisition from bringing interested people back.

recommendations.title: Keep your proven traffic baseline intact
recommendations.whatToDo: Identify the campaigns, audiences, channels, or offers currently producing acceptable results. Keep those stable while you test one meaningful change separately.
recommendations.doneWhen: You have a clearly defined control/baseline that continues running unchanged while the new test runs alongside it.
recommendations.whyCritical: If you change the baseline and the test at the same time, you lose the comparison. You may also disrupt traffic that was already profitable. A stable control lets you protect current performance and learn whether the new idea is genuinely better.

recommendations.title: Run fewer tests with enough budget to learn
recommendations.whatToDo: Choose the highest-value unanswered question and concentrate enough budget and traffic around it to produce a useful result.
recommendations.doneWhen: One clearly defined test has enough budget, traffic, and time to produce a meaningful comparison.
recommendations.whyCritical: Spreading budget across too many audiences, ads, or campaigns can make every test underpowered. Fewer, better-funded tests create cleaner evidence and faster learning.

recommendations.title: Define an acceptable acquisition-cost range.
recommendations.whatToDo: Use customer value, margins, close rate, retention, and repeat purchase behavior.

recommendations.title: Investigate the whole funnel before blaming the channel.
recommendations.whatToDo: Review offer, product mix, merchandising, website, pricing, tracking, promotions, and conversion behavior.

recommendations.title: Reduce dangerous channel concentration.
recommendations.whatToDo: Build a second dependable source without unnecessarily disrupting the first.

recommendations.title: Define your North Star KPIs.
recommendations.whatToDo: Choose the smallest set of metrics that tell you whether marketing is creating meaningful business outcomes.

recommendations.title: Separate outcome KPIs from diagnostic KPIs.
recommendations.whatToDo: Build a hierarchy from business outcome to conversion and supporting diagnostic signals.

recommendations.title: Create a weekly KPI document.
recommendations.whatToDo: Track the same important numbers on a consistent cadence so patterns become visible.

recommendations.title: Define the source of truth for each KPI.
recommendations.whatToDo: Document whether each authoritative number comes from Shopify, CRM, sales, GA4, ad platforms, or another source.

recommendations.title: Connect marketing source to downstream outcomes.
recommendations.whatToDo: Where possible, track source → lead → qualified lead → sale → revenue.

recommendations.title: Keep a simple marketing change log
recommendations.whatToDo: Record the date, what changed, why you changed it, what metric you expected to move, and what actually happened.
recommendations.doneWhen: Each meaningful marketing change has a dated record with the hypothesis, expected impact, and observed result.
recommendations.whyCritical: Without a change log, performance shifts become hard to explain. A simple record helps you connect changes to results and prevents the same failed ideas from being repeated.

recommendations.title: Build a consistent follow-up system.
recommendations.whatToDo: Use email, SMS, retargeting, sales follow-up, abandoned-cart, or nurture where appropriate.

recommendations.title: Review performance across multiple time horizons.
recommendations.whatToDo: Do not let one bad day or week override longer-term trends without investigation.

prompts: Describe what you sell in one sentence without using industry jargon.
What is the single most important result a customer hopes to get from this offer?
Who is most likely to get exceptional value from this offer—and who is not a fit?
What objections come up most often, and what do they reveal about value perception?
What direct evidence—not assumptions—shows that people want this offer?
If traffic doubled tomorrow, what weakness would you be most worried about exposing?
What creates a genuine reason to act now without manufactured scarcity?
Which offer would you keep if you could only sell one for the next 12 months?
Why did recent buyers choose you, and why did recent prospects say no?
What do your best customers have in common beyond demographics?
What tends to happen right before a strong prospect starts looking for help?
Define a qualified lead in one sentence. Then compare your last 20 leads against it.
What larger life or business outcome sits behind the immediate product need?
Where do ideal prospects already spend attention or actively search for solutions?
Which customer group creates the most economic value?
Who should you actively exclude?
How should different segments receive different messages?
What should a relevant stranger understand within five seconds?
For each major feature, ask: “So what does this let the customer do, avoid, gain, or feel?”
Review sales calls, emails, testimonials, and reviews. What phrases appear repeatedly?
Why should a qualified buyer choose you instead of a competitor, DIY, or doing nothing?
What meaningful frustration, ambition, risk, relief, or identity change sits underneath the rational purchase?
Which major claims on your page need stronger proof, and what evidence already exists?
What proof supports each major claim?
Which emotional outcome sits underneath the rational outcome?
What is the one primary action you want a visitor to take?
What are the first three things a visitor sees, and do they justify taking the next step?
Compare the promise before the click with the headline, offer, and CTA after the click. Where does continuity break?
Map every click, page, field, and step between interest and conversion. Which ones are unnecessary?
What reassurance would a skeptical but qualified buyer need immediately before taking action?
What are you asking the visitor to risk—time, money, data, or commitment—and does the experience justify that ask?
Where do visitors drop off?
What proof belongs closer to action?
Is the ask appropriate for the visitor’s current level of trust?
For every meaningful channel, label its primary job: discovery, intent capture, retargeting, nurture, conversion, or reactivation.
What volume enters the top of the funnel, and what proportion becomes the outcomes you care about?
When performance last changed meaningfully, what else changed around the same time?
Where does discovery happen? Where does intent get captured? Where does retargeting or nurture happen?
What single unanswered question would be most valuable to test next, and what baseline would you protect?
What is a new customer economically worth, and what lead/customer acquisition cost can the business sustain?
How concentrated is acquisition in one channel?
Which test would teach you the most without risking the working baseline?
If you could watch only three numbers every week, which would tell you whether marketing is creating real business value?
List your primary outcome KPI, one supporting KPI, and one diagnostic KPI.
What recurring weekly or monthly KPI view would make changes in the business easier to interpret?
For every primary KPI, define one authoritative source and document known attribution differences.
Where does visibility disappear between acquisition, lead quality, sales, and revenue?
What sequence should your team follow before making a major change when performance shifts?
What changed during meaningful performance shifts?
What does sales/customer data say that advertising platforms do not?
What happens to leads after the initial conversion?

cases.title: Making an Existing Introductory Offer Easier to See and Act On
cases.businessModel: Recurring classes, camps, trials, and other programs across multiple locations.
cases.goal: Turn paid traffic into more trial participation and downstream paying families.
cases.situation: A free-trial concept already existed, but acquisition experiences could be broader and less directly focused on that entry offer.
cases.diagnosis: The opportunity was not necessarily to invent a new offer. It was to make the existing offer easier to notice, understand, and act on across ads and landing pages.
cases.intervention: Use clearer free-trial messaging, location-specific landing experiences, stronger CTA visibility, and tighter ad-to-page alignment.
cases.lesson: Sometimes growth comes from reducing the distance between an existing strong offer and the action you want the customer to take.

cases.title: Selling the Outcome Behind the Service
cases.businessModel: Group and 1:1 coaching for professionals, executives, founders, and ambitious learners; historically referral-heavy.
cases.goal: Translate a technically clear service into stronger positioning and acquisition messaging.
cases.situation: The service could easily be interpreted as simply “better English instruction.”
cases.diagnosis: The deeper value included professional confidence, leadership, self-expression, career advancement, and operating effectively in English-speaking environments.
cases.intervention: Center positioning, hooks, landing-page messaging, and customer journeys on those deeper outcomes rather than only the instructional mechanism.
cases.lesson: Customers often buy the life or business outcome created by the service, not merely the mechanism being delivered.

cases.title: Communicating the Integrated Outcome, Not Just the Pieces
cases.businessModel: Done-for-you or assisted branding, websites, CRM, booking, automation, and related business infrastructure.
cases.goal: Make a multi-component service understandable at first glance.
cases.situation: The initial presentation could make the service look disproportionately like website development even though the offer provided much more.
cases.diagnosis: The integrated value was closer to a complete client-acquisition and follow-up system than an isolated website build.
cases.intervention: Shift the hero and supporting messaging toward the end-to-end outcome: look professional, capture leads, book clients, and follow up automatically.
cases.lesson: When a product does several things, communicate the integrated outcome rather than forcing customers to assemble the value themselves.

cases.title: When the Campaign Is Not the Only Problem
cases.businessModel: Programs and educational resources supported by a Google Ad Grant and lead-generation pages.
cases.goal: Improve conversion from search traffic into community/program engagement.
cases.situation: Traffic was being sent to pages where value, forms, and next actions were not always immediately clear.
cases.diagnosis: There was a message and conversion alignment issue between search intent, ad copy, landing-page promise, and conversion action.
cases.intervention: Use benefit-led copy, clearer forms/CTAs, credibility indicators, and tighter page-to-search alignment.
cases.lesson: A traffic source can be functioning while the experience receiving that traffic suppresses results.

cases.title: When Performance “Breaks” Because Measurement Broke
cases.businessModel: Lead-generation campaigns using Google Ads and Google Tag Manager.
cases.diagnosis: A thank-you-page URL change broke the Google Tag Manager trigger.
cases.intervention: Test the form, identify the mismatched URL, update the trigger, republish, and verify the event fires again.
cases.lesson: Sometimes the campaign did not change. Your measurement did.

cases.title: Connecting Paid Media to Downstream Lead Value
cases.businessModel: High-value travel bookings generated from paid and non-paid acquisition sources.
cases.goal: Allocate media based on real lead and sales quality rather than surface conversion volume.
cases.situation: A lead may enter through paid media but later appear as direct, organic, social, or referral depending on the reporting touchpoint.
cases.diagnosis: Platform-level acquisition data alone was insufficient to understand which campaigns ultimately created valuable opportunities.
cases.intervention: Improve the feedback loop between marketing source data and downstream lead/sales outcomes.
cases.lesson: The cheapest lead is not necessarily the most valuable lead; closed-loop reporting helps steer toward real business value.

cases.title: Why One Conversion Column Can Miss the Bigger Picture
cases.businessModel: Multiple retreat and program offerings with cross-pollination between conversion types.
cases.goal: Interpret campaign impact using a broader, more trustworthy measurement view.
cases.situation: A narrow conversion column could make campaign performance appear weaker or more uncertain than broader customer behavior suggested.
cases.diagnosis: Customers converted across multiple programs and conversion types, so one platform column did not capture the full commercial story.
cases.intervention: Review outcome KPIs alongside all-conversion behavior, conversion timing, cross-device and supporting diagnostic metrics.
cases.lesson: Diagnostic metrics provide context to the North Star result; a single platform column rarely tells the entire business story.

cases.title: When “The Ads” May Not Be the Root Cause
cases.businessModel: Direct-to-consumer ecommerce with paid acquisition, merchandising, promotions, and repeat-customer behavior.
cases.goal: Diagnose softer performance without jumping immediately to a channel-level conclusion.
cases.situation: Paid-media performance appeared weaker while product assortment, merchandising, promotions, first-touch customer experience, and traffic mix were also changing.
cases.diagnosis: The issue could be system-level rather than simply “Meta stopped working.”
cases.intervention: Compare business sales, new-customer behavior, merchandising changes, traffic mix, site changes, and platform performance before restructuring the account.
cases.lesson: Marketing channels operate inside a commercial system. When the system changes, ad performance can change even if campaign mechanics are not the root cause.

cases.title: Testing More Things Does Not Always Create More Learning
cases.businessModel: Limited-budget service business testing paid acquisition and creative.
cases.goal: Learn faster without spreading limited budget across too many variables.
cases.situation: Budget is split across multiple campaigns, audiences, creatives, or objectives.
cases.diagnosis: The tests are too underfunded to create meaningful signal, and the working baseline may be destabilized.
cases.intervention: Concentrate budget around fewer hypotheses, preserve the strongest baseline, and document the result.
cases.lesson: Testing more things does not necessarily mean learning more things.

cases.title: When Google and Meta Are Doing Different Jobs
cases.businessModel: A business using intent-based acquisition plus social retargeting.
cases.goal: Evaluate channels based on their contribution to the journey rather than forcing identical expectations.
cases.situation: Channels may be compared independently on immediate sales even though they contribute at different stages.
cases.diagnosis: Google can capture existing intent while Meta reinforces the offer through retargeting and return visits.
cases.intervention: Map channel roles and evaluate the combined journey: intent capture → site visit → retargeting → return → conversion.
cases.lesson: A channel does not have to receive final-touch credit to contribute materially to acquisition.
